pronunciation.note: Ebisu is Tier 2: plain Hepburn. His name may derive from a word for 'foreigner' or 'straggler,' reflecting his origins as a deity associated with outsiders and the sea.

domains.title: God of Fishermen, Commerce, and Honest Luck
domains.subtitle: The Smiling God of Daily Prosperity
domains.lead: Ebisu is the most approachable of Japan's fortune gods. With his fishing rod in one hand and a sea bream (tai) under the other arm, he smiles at merchants, fishermen, and anyone who earns a living by honest work. He is the only native Japanese member of the Seven Gods of Fortune (Shichifukujin).

cards.name: Fisherman God
cards.desc: Patron of those who draw wealth from the sea, especially fishers and seafood merchants.

cards.name: God of Commerce
cards.desc: Protector of markets, shops, and fair dealing in everyday trade.

cards.name: Shichifukujin
cards.desc: The only native kami among the Seven Gods of Fortune.

cards.name: Sea Bream
cards.desc: The tai fish is auspicious because its name puns on 'medetai' (auspicious).

mythology.lead: Ebisu has no single founding myth. He grew from several older figures — the castaway child Hiruko, the oracular Kotoshironushi, and deities of the foreign sea — into the cheerful merchant god of the Edo period.

myths.title: Hiruko, the Leech Child
myths.text: The Kojiki tells that Izanagi and Izanami's first child, Hiruko, was born malformed and set adrift in a boat of reeds. He grew up to become associated with the sea and with outsiders, and later tradition identified him with Ebisu. His survival from abandonment makes him a god of those who make their own way.

myths.title: Kotoshironushi
myths.text: Kotoshironushi, the son of Ōkuninushi, was a god of oracles and fishing who surrendered the land to Amaterasu's descendants and then withdrew to the sea. Some traditions merge him with Ebisu, deepening the connection between the fortune god and the maritime realm.

myths.title: Ebisu the Smiling Merchant
myths.text: By the Edo period, Ebisu had become the patron of shops, fish markets, and the common trades. His image — smiling, holding a fishing rod and a sea bream — was placed near cash registers and shop entrances. The Toka Ebisu festival in Ōsaka remains one of Japan's largest celebrations of commerce and good fortune.

lore.syncretism: Ebisu is a composite. His roots are in the Kojiki figures Hiruko and Kotoshironushi, but his popular form was shaped by merchant culture and the cult of the Seven Gods of Fortune. He is often paired with Daikokuten as a double patron of prosperity, and with Benzaiten as the couple who bless culture and commerce.
lore.culturalLegacy: Ebisu is everywhere in Japanese commercial life: shop signs, sake labels, New Year prints, and the Toka Ebisu festival in Ōsaka. The Yebisu beer brand takes its name and logo from him. He is the god of small business, honest profit, and the daily labor that keeps society fed.
lore.extendedMeditation: Ebisu teaches that prosperity is not reserved for the mighty. The fisherman, the shopkeeper, and the cook all have a fortune god. His smile is a reminder that honest work is itself sacred and that daily bread can be a blessing.

sources.name: Bocking, A Popular Dictionary of Shinto

lore.archaeology: Ebisu is primarily a cultic and commercial figure rather than an archaeological one. His imagery dominates Edo-period shop signs, votive prints (ema), and festival paraphernalia, especially in Ōsaka and fishing ports. The Toka Ebisu festival at Imamiya Ebisu Shrine preserves the material culture of merchant devotion.
